name: Hi-top fade

card.summary: A hairstyle with short faded sides and a tall flat top that adds height and a sharp, geometric head silhouette.

quick.overview:
The hi-top fade pairs closely cropped, faded sides with a longer, raised top, often cut flat. The contrast makes the head look taller and more sculpted.

It rose in the mid-1980s in African American and hip-hop culture, faded in the early 1990s, and has been revived in the 2000s and 2010s. No clinical research addresses it.
quick.how: Barbers fade the sides and shape the top to an even height; the style is described as suited to curly or coily hair and needs frequent trims to keep the lines sharp. Some people wear it with designs or braids.
quick.risks: Little risk beyond razor irritation or ingrown hairs common to close cuts. Upkeep requires regular barber visits to keep the fade crisp.

lead: The hi-top fade has short or closely cropped sides and a longer, raised top. Over time versions became more geometric, with slanted variants such as the gumby and reagan.[1]

It is used to add vertical height and a defined silhouette. It is closely tied to hip hop's golden age and new jack swing: by 1984 it had spread among young African Americans in New York, Washington, Philadelphia and London, and in 1988-89 rappers such as Kid 'N Play and Big Daddy Kane made it iconic.[1]
It fell out of fashion in the early 1990s and returned in the 2000s with athletes such as Iman Shumpert and Nerlens Noel.[1]

chain: Taller, squarer, more defined head silhouette
angle.text: The cut adds perceived height at the crown and strong contrast between sides and top, which people use to change their head shape and give a sharper profile.

paras: The style has tapered sides and a longer top; the geometric variants include slanted shapes.[1]

A 1980 Grace Jones album cover by Jean-Paul Goude showed a flattop precursor, and Schoolly D and Doug E. Fresh wore early versions in 1985. Salt-N-Pepa's 1987 video featured more modern examples.[1] Will Smith wore it on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.[1]
After declining by 1994 in favour of low fades and cornrows, it returned in the 2000s and appeared at Barack Obama's 2013 second inauguration events.[1]

timeline.event: Warm Leatherette cover shows a flattop precursor.[1]
Rappers make the style a symbol of rap culture through 1989.[1]
Urban styles move toward low fades and cornrows.[1]
